reason: The sources provide 14 highly specific, cross-verified claims about the 1626 Wanggongchang Explosion, supported by vivid eyewitness details.
story: On the morning of May 30, 1626, a sudden rumble shattered the peace of Beijing. Seconds later, a blinding flash preceded a catastrophic blast at the Wanggongchang Armory. The imperial gunpowder factory exploded with the force of a modern atomic bomb, obliterating a two-square-kilometer area of the densely populated capital. A towering mushroom cloud rose over the ruined city as debris, iron fragments, and even human remains rained from the sky. Mysteriously, many victims who survived the initial shockwave were found completely stripped of their clothing. The force of the blast was so massive it threw a three-ton stone lion over the city walls and was felt 150 kilometers away. Inside the Forbidden City, the Tianqi Emperor fled his breakfast in terror, but his only infant heir perished in the aftermath. Believing it was divine punishment for imperial incompetence, the emperor issued a public confession of repentance.
angle: The explosion's blast wave was so uniquely violent that it left thousands of victims completely stripped of their clothing and flung a three-ton stone lion over the city walls.

claims.claim: The disaster resulted in the deaths of approximately 20,000 people.

evidence.quote: kills 20,000 people, and enters the annals of history
An estimated 20,000 people perished.

claims.claim: The explosion completely flattened or obliterated an area of about two square kilometers.

evidence.quote: Almost everything within an area of two square kilometers surrounding the site was instantly obliterated.
An area of roughly two square kilometres around the works was flattened

claims.claim: Tremors or sounds from the blast were heard or felt over 150 kilometers away.

evidence.quote: tremblings were felt over 150 kilometres (93 mi) away
was heard beyond the Great Wall over 150 kilometers from the blast site.

claims.claim: A massive cloud resembling a mushroom rose into the sky over the city after the explosion.

evidence.quote: an enormous cloud in the shape of a mushroom rose into the sky.
a cloud that contemporary observers describe as “resembling a mushroom” rose into the sky

claims.claim: The force of the explosion was strong enough to throw a stone lion weighing about 3 tons over a city wall or gate.

evidence.quote: a 5,000-catty (about 3 metric tons) stone lion was thrown over the city wall.
hurled a stone lion weighing nearly three tons over a city gate

claims.claim: Many victims of the explosion were found completely stripped of their clothing.

evidence.quote: The bodies of those victims who didn’t disintegrate straight away were later found stripped of clothing
victims found stripped of their clothing

claims.claim: The Tianqi Emperor was eating breakfast when the explosion happened and had to flee.

evidence.quote: The Tianqi Emperor himself was having breakfast in Qianqing Palace when the explosion occurred.
The Tianqi Emperor, at breakfast, fled through collapsing eaves

claims.claim: The Tianqi Emperor's only remaining heir, infant Crown Prince Zhu Cijiong, died following the disaster.

evidence.quote: The Tianqi Emperor's only remaining heir, the 7-month-old Crown Prince Zhu Cijiong (朱慈炅), died from the shock.
his infant son and only heir, the crown prince Zhu Cijiong, died in the disaster’s aftermath

claims.claim: Following the explosion, the Tianqi Emperor was forced to issue a repenting edict and allocate 20,000 taels of gold for relief.

evidence.quote: Tianqi Emperor was forced to publicly announce a repenting edict, and issued 20,000 taels of gold for the rescue and relief effort.
He directed the disbursement of 20,000 taels of gold for victim relief and reconstruction

claims.claim: Many contemporaries and the court interpreted the catastrophe as a warning or punishment from Heaven due to the emperor's misrule.

evidence.quote: believed that the incident was a punishment from Heaven as a warning to correct the sins of the emperor's personal incompetence.
the Wanggongchang Explosion was widely interpreted by contemporaries as a manifestation of heavenly retribution, reflecting the traditional Chinese belief in the Mandate of Heaven

claims.claim: The Wanggongchang facility was normally staffed by 70 to 80 personnel.

evidence.quote: It was normally staffed by 70 to 80 personnel.
the armories were staffed by between 70 and 80 people

claims.claim: The ground at the epicenter subsided dramatically to form a deep depression or crater.

evidence.quote: The ground around the immediate vicinity of Wanggongchang Armory, the epicenter of the explosion, had sunk over 2 zhàngs
At the epicenter, the ground subsided dramatically, forming a crater approximately 20 feet deep

disputed: The exact physical cause of the explosion remains unresolved. While an accidental gunpowder ignition is the standard historical consensus, other hypothesized theories include a meteor air burst, a natural gas leak, a volcanic eruption, or an earthquake releasing ignited gases. The script should present gunpowder as the leading theory while presenting the others as historical speculations.

The physical effects of the blast on victims' bodies are described with varying degrees of sensationalism. Some contemporary accounts detail gruesome raining of body parts and blood, while others focus on victims being stripped of clothing. A script should handle the rain of body parts with caution and focus on the documented blast wave stripping clothing.
